It , did not, however, last long—a fact due, it is said, to the in- . Wanes of Abdurrahman, who lee sun 4 Afsal. Alnal was / arrested, and Abdurrahman tweed himself from. MIAMI= by pounds, shillings, and pence, the coat of the policy of the late Government in provoking a grievance with the late Ameer of Afghanint to, and of attempting to steal a slice of his territory to make a "scientific frontier " to gratify a whim of Lord Bea- consfield, is now known; but the coat in life, limb, and human misery, which lies at the door of the late Ad• ministration, will never be lmown to mortals. The bodice that lie bleaching on the mountain elopes and in the valleys of Afghanistan, and the widows and orphans that bemoan the loss of huebanda and fathers— escrifiees to an 'mane and creel policy—will never be correctly tallied; and it will be long before the hatred and jealousy of a people which profeeees to be the most religiou. and honourable on the fare of the earth, audit. foremost in the rank of civilised nations, have been erased from the hearts and minds of outraged Afghane, whose desolated homee and neglected fields remind them of an *wet interference with their dorneetie peace. The late Governtoent frequently mewed the multi y that the eoet of the Afghan out- rage would be comparatively trifling, and that the scientific frontier" was an accomplished thing. Both statements were, however, utterly without foundation. As 800 a as the late Government threw up the reins of elate, the country was startled by a telegraphic message from India that there was • deficit of about four million pounds eterling, and not a single apologist has yet arieen for this unperdonable financial blunder. Later investigations have revealed the unwelcome fact that—leaving out of the reekening the emit of the reverses at Candahar—the expense of our filibuster- ing expedition in Afghaniatan will be about three times ae much no it was alleged to be lees than ale months ago. The telegram announcing the deficit of £4,000,000 was received from Simla in May, and it stated that the discovery of an error in the estimateo showed the total met of the war up to that period to be £10,000,000. In February • financial statement had Men put before the Legislative Council of India that the total war eteptusee up to that period had been £5,970,000, rid which sum £670,000 had been spent in the years 1878.9, £3,216,000 in 1879-80, and £3,090,000 to £lBBO.l. In the Indian Budget statement which the Marquis of Harrington placed before the House of Commons on Tuesday evening, in a speech which has elicited eneomitims from both political I rieods and opponents, be apprieed the Home that the Simla telegram of May ought to have pat the emit of the war at that period at £15,000,000 and Lot at £10,000,000. From thin his Lordship made an allowance of a million for railway traffic/ and telegrams due directly to the war, thus reducing the figure to £14,000,000. He, however, added to this large sum .C 4,184,000 for frontier railways m a part • the mat of the war, and this addition is justified by the apprelieneion that the railways will not payee an investment in times of peace. A final total, there• fore, is reached of over £18,000,000, or over e 8,000,000 more than the sum named in the Simla telegram, which acknowledged • deficit of £4,000,000. Had, said Lord Harrington, no charges arisen in connection with this blundering, there would have been, swing to the improved tiondition of Indian finanoes, a stir- plua during the lad three years of £11,000,000. De- ducting from the £18,000,000 this supposed surplus of £11,000,000, there remain, on the three years • deficit of £7,000,000. Somebody blundered in framing the estimates. At fleet the excuoe given wee that the disparity had aria= from the unforeseen nemesity of havingto purohme,matead of hiring,the means of tram. poet, and of having to pey exorbitant price. for grain. It transpires, however, that the blunder is not to be deposed of by such allegations ae these, but that it to be found in the accounts of the military departmemh ot which the chief officers of the Government aught to have known more than they seem to have done, eeeeng that the Iced exchequere in the north-west had been emptied of their mually Large Wanees in order to furnish the sinews of war. The Marquis of Harting- stated in unvarnished teems that there must have been a " rookies& determination to uoder-estimate the difft• eulties of the enterprise,' and that he oould not acquit the members of the Supreme Government of eogli- genoe, and even of something approaching to blind- nese, in allowing themselves to suppooe that a war lasting so keg, and conducted on so large a scale, and in such a distant and difficult eountry, could be carried on at so trifling a cast as they bid estimated. But the war is not ended yet, and what the total oost of the "scientific frontier" eenapade will be to the Indian and English exchequers no man can com- pute. That England is to hear part of the war bill, the home Government have defieitely decided ; and in arriving at this decisbei the Government nay that they have been booed to set consistently with the public dedarations of Lord 13oaconsfield when in office that the war was entered upon for iraperial purposes. If the Indian authoritiee had been left to thermelves they would never have dreamed of a " scientific frontier" ; Lord Beaconsfield, had he fulfilled hie promise of looking after sanitary matters indeed of miming himself with oriental baublm, would never bave dreamed of a "scientific frontier" either; and the reeult would have been no war in Afghanistan, no wholesale destruction of human life, no maimiUtt and crippling of brave fellows, no widows seed orphans musing the authors of war and deploring its horror., and no mach fiscal muddle ea that which is now puzzling both Eaglish and Indian financier, But we are in the thick of the conflict, and we mast endeavour to come out of it with our spur.; and with as moth honour as our wrong -headed- nem will admit of. In future the war has to be paid out of current revenue, and this has been done for the last four month.. To do thin, however, it is likely the Indian Government will have to borrow funds, and until the war it nettled aad it. omit known, it will be impossible to any what proportions the English people and the Indians iball pay for provoking and carrying on a war

Which neither reason nor justios one defend. The dory told by Lord Harlington was put before the Boom of Commons in a most statesmanlike manner , and happily it. seduces was relieved by the consoling hope that the finance. of India will ere long be raised from their chaotic state into a more estlafactory and fiouriahing condition.

Speeches like that which Mr. :Dillon, the member for Tipperary, delivered the other day al Kilave, will not hasten relief to the distrait/ad distriete of Ireland, nor adv.oa the cause of those whom the Irish Come peasation Disturbance Bill would have beneSted had it passed through instead of being strangled in the House of Lords. Whilst we sympathise with the distremed farmers of Ireland in being deprived of the fall advantage of improvements they have effected in another man's soil when overtaken by a eueemeion of bad harvests, and no fixed aa to be enable to pay route ; but we have no patience with much blatant agitators aa Mr. Dillon is, and who endeavour to persuade an excited people that landowners have not some legal interest in the land and as much right to enjoy as tenants have the value of inveetments whether acquired or hereditary in the land. To tell an excited amembly of men, ready to throw off all restraint., of order and pea., that such a gathering "ust strike fear into the enemies of the people and into the man who dreamed of turning a Kildare man out of his hem" is to invite a display of rowdyism and bad passions. Could • more insurrectionary speech be delivered than that front which we extract the following : ‘. The House of fords had taught them thatnogood would come 001 00 London to Ireland, and that until the Irish people, on the fields of Ireland, were banded together in ea organisation fitted to win the battle for thenwelves, they could not expect Justice or fair play or good laws from an English Parliament. The country should be so well ' organised that every farmer should belong to a branch of the Land League, and the young farmersthould be prepared ! to march to the meetings and in proper order too. And , when they had that organisation perfected, let the wora go , out that no farm from which any man had been evicted ! should be touched or need for human purposes until its rightful owner WLS put back upon the soil. In the county of Mayo, where the organisation was now pretty strong, they had many farms lying idle from which landlords could draw no rent, because they had evicted tenants from them ; nor if the landlord pot cattle on them would the cattle prosper very much. They most teach the landlords that if they evicted tenants they would not be the richer, hot the poorer. (ft voice: We Will show them something that they know nothing about yet.) Mr. Dillon said that if any man took • farm from which another had been evicted, there were a hundred ways in which the farmers could show him that it would have been better for him not to have taken that farm. Without raising a linger to harm him they could make his possession an exceeding uncomfortable one, and oar that he would be very glad to give up before bog. (Hear, hear, and cheers.) The people should be Invited to join the Land League, and If anyone refused to do so his neighbours would know that he had turned his back up. the people. But he believed that nine out of ten would join it. It 'meld be their business to report how litany men could march to the ineetings, and they should be able to do eti like a regiment of soldier. There would be more effect in MO young men marching to a meeting under the command of their leaders than is twenty sixeches. (Cheers.) And he would tell them what the League would do if the landlords refused justice to the people for another six menthe of the year. When they should have enrolled 300,000 member, of the League, if the landlords should persist in refusing the moderate demands of the people, they would give out the word to the people of Ireland to strike against rent altogether, and pay no more until justice was done to them. (Cheers.) With 300,000 Irishnien enrolled an members of the Land League, all the armies of England would not levy rent in this country. (hood cheers.) And then they would ask harder terms from the landlords. fie could tell the noble lords, whom be heard the other night denouncing "irresponsible Celtic agita- tors," that, much as thejr disliked the Compensation for Piaturbance Bill, before another year went by they would tint themselves compelled to accept • bill which they would dislike much more. (Cheers.) Let them adopt the platform of the Land League—namely, the land for the people and an opportunity for every farmer to rooks himself, if he liked to do so, the owner of his hold- ing. (Cheers.) folks mmntime the representatives of the pepole could paralyse the hand of Government, and prevent them from passing laws that would throw the people into prison for organising themselves. They could obetruct the passing of coercive laws and set the people free to drill them- selves and organise themaelves. They could Übe it out of the power of the police to arrest any man who was out after eight o'clock at night. They would see that Irishmen had a right to be out after eight o'clock, and all tbe night through if they thought tit. (Cheers.) They had a right to march to their meetings and to obey the commands of their leaders, if they chose to do so. They would see that every man in Ireland had • right to have a rifle if he liked. (Cheers.) All that he could say was that if the nunhood of Ireland was not enough when they had their Highs to win their freedom and so put down landlordism, then he should he ashamed to call himself en Irishman. Let the people of Kildare short during the corning autumn that neither dukes nor marquiser nor any other lords could terrorise or intirni. date the manhood of their great country.

Iv is not to bewondered atthatMr. Forster, when the attention of the House of Commons was on Tueeday directed to Mr. Dillon's utterances, ehonld have charac- terised there as wicked and cos selly—aowarelly in .peeking in term. that protected him from prosecu- tion for eedition and yet invited a discontented people to insurrection. Violence and reeietance to Government will postpone reforms that Ireland un• doubtedly etands in need of ill her land laws, and will increase the misery which the people ere at present etiffering. If the Irish tenantry are wronged by evictions from their holdings without receiving compensation for any unexhatteted improvements they may have effected, it is no excuse for them to perpetrate another wrong by resorting to the destruction of life by rifle and ,het, and perpetus • ting anarchy in the country. If they suspent that they are by violence about to mowed in denying the landowners of their just rights, it is time they were aseured that they will no more be per. milted to do this than the landlords will in the near future ho allowed to exact from the tenants that which they are not in jugtice entitled to. The present Government have proved themselves the friends of the Irish people, and the latter may oonfidently look to the former, if encouraged, to con- Untie their just and kindly efforts in the future; bat that Government will be no more disposed to tolerate •wroug upon the landowner, than they will to countenence the infliction of injustice upon the tenantry. The Government, as executants of the law as it exists, will compel the observance of order, and as the quelling of diaturbanoes means expenee and misery, and the dietraotion of the minds of legislators from the framing of laws, the adoption of such wretched hints as those contained in Mr. Dillon', speech will lead to the increase of national hurddne and:the delay of measures of justice, which the present Liberal Government will undoubtedly press forward, in the only legitimate way in which they can be put upon the etatute book.

TOWN TALK. The Nonconformist Sunday echools in Widnes have decided to celebrate the centenary on the 2filth instant. Those who have the carrying out the arrangements will find it. very difficult matter, to equal, without ever dr ing of eclipeing, the success of the proceedings in the neigh- bouring town of Runcorn. 11. stated that a very important legal struggle is likely to take place between the Widnes Local Board and the prn- perty owners on the West Bank Estate. A very considerable sum is owing for drainage by the ratepayers, and I under- stand that a sort of association has been formed for the purpose of taking conosels' opinion on the liability of the property owners, who hold that in the present state of matters they are being charged twice for drainage. They also state that they will object to pay anything on account of the new sewaze scheme, concerning which a Local Go- vernment Boord inquiry woe lately held in Widnes, and to carry out which it is proposed to borrow the sum of £40,000. The rumour is gaining eome ground that the last-named -cheme will not be carrird O. immediately, a.s was some short time ago supposed. 1 How is a that men who are perpetually professing note- Orally ia politics and religion are everlastingly dabbling in tooth:' Here is a nice little bit of election literature, which ne of your Liverpool contemporaries published during the recent election in that town Among the many certificates

of character given to Lord Claud Joh;Hamilton during the present content in one from 'A. Mackie,' which a Comervm tire contemporary print, in big type. This gentleman testi- fies not only to • young Claud's' public career, hut also to , the fireumetance that he is one of 'Om handeonae tons.' All this in very delightful but who in 'A. Mackin'? I Is he the gentleman who wan thought good enough by the Carlton Club to send dawn to Perth to experience a certain thrashing? Now that '.O. Mackie' has come forward in to handmine a manner to testify to the splendid social and I political success of his friend 'young Claud,' perhaps his I lordahip will be good enough to -return the compliment by I urniehing the public with some information an to the identity of 'A. Mackie.' Oh, will he? Not evetly. Inn% it enough that the 'handsome Hamilton,' should have been able to eecure such credentials, without an impertinent question being put an to the identity of. man? The writer of the above choice selection of literature must surely have been reading up Thomas Carlyle, who sore :—.Readere and men generally are getting into strange habits of totting all persons and things, from poor editor's books, up to church dignitsries and state potentates—not 'By what designation art thou called?' In what wig and triangle dost thou walk abroad? Heavens! I know thy designation end black triangle well enough but what in Ood's mune art then fo, VLArViln

There is a particular corner of En ;land where a singular prejudice appears to prevail among a considerable pronto- lion of the people, inclnding suns educated penning against the School Board—en institution which, in all other parts of the country ...gide of exclusively sectarian circles, is generally popular. 'The exceptional region to which we refer extend. over much of the arm of Cheshire, and touches in place, upon Lancishire. Cheerer, the capital of the anti- School Boanl country, takeathe affection in a comparatively mild form other more or less fopolooc centres are SPmk- port, Stalybridge, and Congleton, and in each there has been a movement for the aholition of the School Board—a move- ment which in the single case nf Stockport wee pushed to extremities by hard party feeling and resulted in the diss,o, lotion of the Hostd. Another somewhat important centre is Warrington, an here the superstition against the Soho° Board takes a very peculiar shape. In Stockport, Maly- bridge, and Congleton the argument was that there wu voluntary wheel accommodation enough, end therefore the School 11na.,1 was not nemsaarv. and though in each instance the contention as to accommodation was not satisfactorily made out, no official proof has one been given of such a de- ficiency of euimhle schooling es to render the existence of a SCIIOOI Board a 14441 necessity. If ,n Stockport it had been made clear to demonstration 'that there were not full and proper facilities for the clumtion of the children, the ene- rnim of the School Board would, it appeared, have given up the contest, and have ceased to clamour for the application of Mr. Pell'. Clause. But in Warrington the conditions are reversed. There no School Board in Warrindon the School Attendance Committee has proved itself quite inca- pable of grappling with the work of attendance ; there are a thrupsend children not found in any ach ol ; and the anew, mai dion, if not absolutely insufficieot, is admittedly and notoriously unsuitable to the thousand children whnin the Attendance Committeo appear to he not even trying tenet! into the schools. This would therefore seem to he clown /menially and peculierly calling for the establishment of a School Board. Them is a degree of earnestness in the , borough of 4 certain kind in favour of education; a pamatile ! amount of schooling has been carried on in thetrown in times past, nf a sectarian character: the members of the Town ! Council, of whatever nolitiml piety, recognise the grievous defects of the mCating Mate of things, and do net &tor that I what is wanted in jure what a School Board would a. and , what 11. e Attendance Committee cannot do. And! what in the result of this state of things? Not, as anybaly would immediately suggest, • demand for the election of a Schaal Board, but a strong appeal to the powers that be to confer upon the We,. rington Attendance Committ as the functions of a School Idwrd. The mysteriou prejudice ageing the School Board : in the (anent the Net that a School Board in the one thing needful in Warrington, has driven the Town Council to plaintive omen's to the Government roach Parliament to give Warrington a School Beard under the name and dia, amiss of a School Attendance Committee. And this feeling ism strong in the Council that, though there is row not the elightmt ground for hope that any such unreasonable end unmeaning thing will ever be done at Westminster—for Mr. has told some of these gentleinen the, the notion I ie entirely out of the mu...Bon—the Council have just re- , solved, by uncle of twenty membere againet six, that they will not ask the Committee of Council on Erlumtion to ifl.no en enter for the election 010 School Beard. There was, of of course, ann.! deal of fon,ish talk at the Council meeting almut the coot off School Board • but it must hare been evident In thew who ere not blinded by this phenomenal dread of the School Board.that an Attend .nre Committee gifted with School Hoard power,. wool.] anent exactly as much money ns the School Board in performing the work of the School Board. There is left, we may admit, the arguinent that. under the sinewl ir notion of the subject en- tertained by the Warrington Town Council, the institution under the name of an Attendance Committee, invested with the powers of a School Board, would differ from a reel School Board in the one point that the School Board would he elected by the people and represent the people, while the so.cilled Attendance Committee would be nothing more after all thin a sob-committee of the Town Council.
